name: Ipratropium bromide
route_note: Inhaler or nebuliser 3–4 times daily; nasal spray for rhinorrhoea

discovery.note: An N-isopropyl quaternary derivative of atropine, designed to keep anticholinergic bronchodilation while minimising systemic absorption.

tagline: Short-acting inhaled anticholinergic for COPD, acute asthma and runny nose
summary: Ipratropium bromide is a quaternary atropine derivative that blocks muscarinic receptors in the airways. It is used by inhalation for COPD and, together with salbutamol, in acute severe asthma, and as a nasal spray for rhinorrhoea.
mechanism: Ipratropium competitively antagonises acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle and submucosal glands, reducing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction and secretions.
It is non-selective across M1–M3 subtypes and acts for 4–6 hours. Its quaternary nitrogen keeps it charged, so little crosses mucosal membranes or the blood–brain barrier.
uses: Rhinorrhoea of allergic and non-allergic rhinitis and the common cold (nasal spray)

history.title: Introduced
history.detail: Atrovent enters medical use in Germany.

history.title: Combivent
history.detail: FDA approves the ipratropium/albuterol combination inhaler Combivent.

history.title: Soft-mist inhaler
history.detail: Combivent Respimat is approved in the US, replacing the CFC aerosol.

serious: Acute angle-closure glaucoma if nebulised into the eyes

facts: Ipratropium is derived from atropine, the alkaloid of Atropa belladonna, whose smoke was once inhaled for asthma.
Its successor tiotropium, also from Boehringer Ingelheim, allows once-daily dosing.
